overview:
Colonial scholarship, in the context of Jain studies, refers to the body of knowledge about Jainism produced during the period of European imperial expansion in South Asia, roughly from the late eighteenth to the mid‑twentieth century. This scholarship emerged from the intersecting activities of colonial administrators, Orientalist philologists, Christian missionaries, and increasingly, Jain lay leaders and monks who acted as informants, patrons, and collaborators. It was shaped by the priorities of the colonial state, the taxonomic ambitions of European academia, and the internal dynamics of Jain communities responding to new forms of power and representation.

Early colonial encounters with Jainism were often incidental to administrative and commercial concerns. Figures such as Alexander Walker of Bowland, James Tod, and other East India Company officials encountered Jains as merchants, bankers, and local elites, and only gradually came to recognize them as adherents of a distinct religious tradition rather than a sub‑group of “Hindus” or “Banias.” Their reports, memoranda, and ethnographic notes—frequently unpublished or scattered in archives—constitute some of the earliest sustained English‑language descriptions of Jain practices, temples, and doctrines. These materials were deeply shaped by the colonial gaze: they foregrounded economic roles, legal disputes, and political alliances, while often misunderstanding or simplifying doctrinal subtleties and sectarian distinctions.

Alongside administrators, Orientalist scholars in Calcutta, Madras, Bombay, and later in European universities began to focus on Jain canonical and philosophical texts. The nineteenth century saw the first critical editions and translations of key works such as the Kalpa‑sūtra, Āvaśyaka‑literature, and portions of the Śvetāmbara canon, as well as Digambara philosophical treatises. Hermann Jacobi’s 1879 edition and translation of the Kalpa‑sūtra is often cited as a pivotal moment when Jainism was more clearly recognized in European scholarship as a distinct religious tradition rather than merely a heterodox branch of Hinduism or Buddhism. These philological projects relied heavily on manuscripts, oral explanations, and textual guidance provided by Jain monks and lay scholars, even though the resulting publications were framed within European academic norms and often detached from living ritual contexts.

Missionary writings formed another strand of colonial scholarship. Christian missionaries in South India, Gujarat, Rajasthan, and elsewhere produced polemical tracts, sermons, and ethnographic accounts that described Jain doctrines and practices in order to critique them and promote conversion. These texts frequently emphasized themes such as image‑worship, asceticism, and karma, but interpreted them through Christian theological lenses, sometimes portraying Jainism as excessively legalistic, world‑denying, or morally rigorous. Later Orientalists and administrators sometimes drew on these missionary accounts, reproducing their misunderstandings and biases even when their own aims were more descriptive than polemical.

From the late nineteenth century into the early twentieth, Jain actors increasingly shaped colonial scholarship. Wealthy Jain merchants and philanthropists funded printing presses, sponsored editions of Prakrit and Sanskrit texts, and supported European and Indian scholars who worked on Jain materials. Monks and lay pandits provided authoritative recensions of texts, corrected translations, and debated doctrinal interpretations. This period saw the emergence of Jainological studies as a recognizable academic field, with contributions from German, Italian, American, and Indian scholars who produced grammars, catalogues, doctrinal surveys, and historical narratives. At the same time, Jain communities used colonial legal and educational structures to articulate and defend their religious identity, for example in court cases over temple control, image‑worship, and sectarian boundaries.

Colonial scholarship on Jainism thus has a double legacy. On one hand, it preserved, catalogued, and made accessible a vast corpus of Jain texts and inscriptions, laying foundations for modern academic Jainology and for many contemporary community publications. On the other hand, it introduced enduring distortions: overemphasis on texts at the expense of lived practice; privileging certain sects or regions; framing Jainism primarily through categories such as “world‑renouncing asceticism” or “merchant ethics”; and embedding Jain narratives within colonial hierarchies of knowledge. Modern scholarship and community education increasingly revisit colonial‑era sources critically, highlighting the collaborative roles of Jain informants and patrons, exposing missionary and Orientalist biases, and re‑situating Jainism within its own intellectual and ritual horizons rather than solely within colonial taxonomies.

For Jain studies today, “colonial scholarship” is therefore not simply a historical label but a methodological caution. It reminds researchers and practitioners to distinguish between primary Jain sources and the interpretive frameworks imposed by colonial contexts; to trace how categories like “religion,” “sect,” and “canon” were reshaped under imperial rule; and to recognize both the contributions and the limitations of nineteenth‑ and early twentieth‑century Jainological work. It also invites renewed attention to archival materials—letters, reports, court records, missionary tracts—that document how Jains themselves navigated colonial power, contested misrepresentations, and cooperated strategically to ensure the survival and transmission of their tradition.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; edited and translated by Hermann Jacobi in the colonial period
primary_sources.original_text: णमो अरिहंताणं, णमो सिद्धाणं, णमो आयरियाणं, णमो उवज्झायाणं, णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ, ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ, ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ
primary_sources.translation: Homage to the Arhats, homage to the Siddhas, homage to the Ācāryas, homage to the Upādhyāyas, homage to all the Sādhus in the world.
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa‑sūtra is a key Śvetāmbara canonical text, recited especially during Paryuṣaṇa. Hermann Jacobi’s 1879 critical edition and German translation, produced within a colonial and Orientalist framework, became foundational for European recognition of Jainism as a distinct religion. Jacobi’s work relied on manuscripts and guidance from Jain monks, yet it also exemplifies colonial philological priorities: focus on textual authenticity, historical dating of Mahāvīra, and comparison with Buddhist and Brahmanical sources. Modern scholars and Jain communities continue to use Jacobi’s edition while also consulting traditional commentaries and living recitation practices to correct or contextualize his interpretations.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha-sūtra (Tattvārthādhigama)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: Right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct constitute the path to liberation.
primary_sources.notes: The Tattvārtha‑sūtra is a central philosophical text accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions. Colonial scholars, including European Indologists, produced editions, translations, and studies of this work to systematize Jain doctrine in terms familiar to Western philosophy and comparative religion. Their readings often emphasized abstract metaphysics and ethics, sometimes underplaying ritual, narrative, and sectarian commentarial traditions. Jain pandits and monks collaborated by providing manuscripts, explanations, and traditional exegesis, which modern scholarship increasingly foregrounds to balance colonial interpretations.

primary_sources.title: Āvaśyaka-sūtra (selected verse)
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara text; multiple redactors
primary_sources.original_text: मित्ति मे सव्वभूएसु, वेरं मज्झं न केणइ
primary_sources.transliteration: mitti me savvabhūesu, veraṃ majjhaṃ na keṇai
primary_sources.translation: May I have friendship with all living beings; may I have enmity with none.
primary_sources.notes: Verses from the Āvaśyaka‑sūtra, such as this declaration of universal friendship, were frequently cited by colonial scholars and missionaries to characterize Jain ethics of non‑violence. Orientalist editions and translations sometimes extracted such verses from their ritual and meditative contexts, presenting them as isolated moral aphorisms. Jain teachers, both in the colonial period and today, situate these lines within a broader liturgical cycle, emphasizing their role in daily practice, confession, and cultivation of ahiṃsā rather than merely as abstract ethical statements.

misconceptions.myth: Colonial scholars independently discovered Jainism and defined it as a distinct religion without significant input from Jains themselves.
misconceptions.reality: While colonial administrators, Orientalists, and missionaries played major roles in cataloguing and classifying Jain texts and practices, they did so in constant interaction with Jain merchants, monks, and lay scholars. Jain informants provided doctrinal explanations, corrected misunderstandings, supplied manuscripts, and funded publications. Recent research shows that Jains were active agents in shaping how their tradition was presented, even though colonial frameworks often obscured or minimized this collaboration.

misconceptions.myth: Colonial scholarship offers a neutral, objective account of Jainism that can be used uncritically as the foundation for modern understanding.
misconceptions.reality: Colonial‑era writings are deeply marked by the priorities and biases of their time: the needs of the colonial state, Christian missionary agendas, Orientalist taxonomies, and European philosophical categories. These influences led to distortions, such as overemphasis on textual canon over lived practice, misclassification of sects, and framing Jainism primarily through asceticism or merchant ethics. Modern Jain studies treat colonial sources as valuable but partial, requiring careful comparison with primary Jain texts, traditional commentaries, and contemporary community perspectives.

misconceptions.myth: Missionary accounts of Jainism can be treated as straightforward ethnographic descriptions of Jain belief and practice.
misconceptions.reality: Missionary writings were produced with explicit theological and polemical aims: to critique Jain doctrines and promote Christian conversion. They often misrepresented key concepts like karma, ahiṃsā, and image‑worship, and judged Jain practices against Christian norms. Although these texts contain observations about temples, rituals, and social life, they must be read critically and cross‑checked with Jain sources and more balanced scholarship to avoid reproducing their biases.

misconceptions.myth: The colonial period was only a time of decline and distortion for Jainism, with little positive contribution to Jain learning.
misconceptions.reality: The colonial era certainly introduced new pressures and misrepresentations, but it also saw significant Jain initiatives in education, printing, philanthropy, and legal advocacy. Jain patrons supported presses and libraries, sponsored editions of canonical and philosophical texts, and collaborated with scholars to preserve manuscripts. Court cases and public debates helped articulate Jain identity in new ways. Recognizing these contributions allows a more nuanced view of colonial scholarship as a complex field of cooperation, contestation, and creativity rather than simply a story of decline.
